Scars and keloids

A sham-controlled thyroidectomy trial found improved overall scar ratings and less pain at six months. Other small studies report changes in selected scar measures, while evidence for established keloids and lasting recurrence prevention remains limited.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A sham-controlled thyroidectomy trial found improved overall scar ratings and less pain at six months. Other small studies report changes in selected scar measures, while evidence for established keloids and lasting recurrence prevention remains limited.

Summary of the Evidence

The scar categories contain 31 unique titles: 16 primary human reports, three reviews, one network meta-analysis, two protocols, and nine laboratory studies. The human reports include six randomized trials, six other controlled or uncontrolled studies, two case reports, and two case series. Two 2017 pediatric publications have closely matching authors and designs in 15 children and may report the same cohort. Reviews and the network analysis reuse primary studies; their totals are not additional patient groups. No dedicated animal scar study is filed in the exact category.

Human and clinical evidence

A double-blind, sham-controlled trial of 43 people after thyroidectomy found higher patient satisfaction and global scar ratings, lower pain scores, and lower total Vancouver Scar Scale scores with 830-nm LED treatment at six months. Measured scar color, height, pigmentation, and vascularity also improved numerically more, but those individual differences were not statistically clear (Kim et al. 2022).

Other small controlled studies have examined surgical, burn, cleft-lip, and pediatric scars. A split-scar trial using 633-nm red light at several fluences favored selected observer ratings or pliability measures, but did not find a clear overall pliability difference across all settings. Pediatric reports described lower scar scores and ultrasound thickness; the two publications may overlap. These outcomes concern different scar types and should not be treated as replications of one identical effect. Small case reports and series describe improvement in hypertrophic scars or keloids, but they cannot establish comparative efficacy. A planned perioperative keloid trial is a protocol, not an outcome report.

Animal evidence

No dedicated animal model of keloid or human scar treatment was identified in the exact categories. A related mouse wound experiment reported better repair with sequential red and blue light, but it did not directly test established scars.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Nine laboratory studies report wavelength- and dose-dependent responses in keloid or hypertrophic-scar fibroblasts. Several found reduced cell proliferation, collagen production, or profibrotic signaling. One 660-nm experiment instead reported increased scar-fibroblast counts. These results show that laboratory effects are not uniformly suppressive and do not by themselves predict clinical scar appearance.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical studies used red visible light near 633 nm and near-infrared devices near 830 or 905 nm. The thyroidectomy trial began one week after surgery and treated for four weeks. Other protocols varied in fluence, timing, and session schedule. No head-to-head dose-finding study identifies an optimal wavelength or dose, and evidence for new surgical scars is more developed than evidence for persistent keloids or recurrence.

Interpretation

For early thyroidectomy scars, the sham-controlled study found better overall scores and less pain, while some individual appearance measures were not clearly different. Other trials support selected improvements, but clinical findings cannot yet be generalized to all scar types. The available evidence is weaker for treating established keloids or preventing recurrence.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for selected short-term improvements in early postsurgical scar scores and pain Low for established keloids and long-term recurrence prevention
Publications and records31 unique titles (current Scars clinical + preclinical categories; existing Description lists 17)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A sham-controlled thyroidectomy trial found better six-month patient and clinician ratings, less pain, and lower overall scar scores, while other small studies report improvement in selected measures. The studies vary by scar type and protocol, and some reports may share participants. Independent trials focused on established keloids and longer follow-up would support a stronger conclusion.
